title: Verbs that know whether you're a man or a woman
goal: Describe daily routines with کرتا ہوں / کرتی ہوں — and accept that Urdu verbs change to match the gender of whoever is doing the action.
bekal: build habitual sentences with stem + تا/تی/تے + ہوں/ہے/ہیں
make habitual sentences negative with نہیں
describe a whole day, from getting up to going to bed

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — ایک عام دن
dialogs.intro: Ayesha and Budi are waiting for class to start. The conversation turns to their daily routines.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: آپ صبح کتنے بجے اٹھتے ہیں؟
lines.baca: āp subh kitne baje uṭhte haiñ?
lines.id: What time do you get up in the morning?
lines.literal: you morning how-many o'clock rise are?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: میں چھ بجے اٹھتا ہوں۔ آپ؟
lines.baca: maiñ chhe baje uṭhtā hūñ. āp?
lines.id: I get up at six. You?
lines.literal: I six o'clock rise-(m) am. you?

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: میں پانچ بجے اٹھتی ہوں اور نماز پڑھتی ہوں۔
lines.baca: maiñ pāñch baje uṭhtī hūñ aur namāz paṛhtī hūñ.
lines.id: I get up at five and say my prayers.
lines.literal: I five o'clock rise-(f) am and prayer read-(f) am.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: میں ناشتہ کرتی ہوں اور یونیورسٹی جاتی ہوں۔
lines.baca: maiñ nāshta kartī hūñ aur yūnīvarsiṭī jātī hūñ.
lines.id: I have breakfast and go to the university.
lines.literal: I breakfast do-(f) am and university go-(f) am.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: پراٹھا اور چائے۔ میں انڈے نہیں کھاتی۔
lines.baca: parāṭhā aur chāe. maiñ anḍe nahīñ khātī.
lines.id: Paratha and tea. I don't eat eggs.
lines.literal: paratha and tea. I eggs not eat-(f).

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: میں روز چاول کھاتا ہوں۔ انڈونیشیا میں یہ عام ہے۔
lines.baca: maiñ roz chāval khātā hūñ. Inḍonesiyā meñ ye ām hai.
lines.id: I eat rice every day. That's normal in Indonesia.
lines.literal: I daily rice eat-(m) am. Indonesia in this common is.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: صبح بھی؟ ہم صبح چاول نہیں کھاتے۔
lines.baca: subh bhī? ham subh chāval nahīñ khāte.
lines.id: In the morning too? We don't eat rice in the morning.
lines.literal: morning also? we morning rice not eat-(pl).

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: جی ہاں! شام کو میں اردو پڑھتا ہوں۔
lines.baca: jī hāñ! shām ko maiñ urdū paṛhtā hūñ.
lines.id: Yes! In the evening I study Urdu.
lines.literal: yes yes! evening at I Urdu read-(m) am.

lines.speaker: عائشہ:
lines.text: آپ بہت محنت کرتے ہیں۔ اسی لیے آپ کی اردو اچھی ہے۔
lines.baca: āp bahut mehnat karte haiñ. isī liye āp kī urdū achchhī hai.
lines.id: You work really hard. That's why your Urdu is good.
lines.literal: you very hard-work do-(pl) are. that-very for you of-(f) Urdu good is.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: شکریہ۔ لیکن میں ابھی بہت غلطیاں کرتا ہوں۔
lines.baca: shukriya. lekin maiñ abhī bahut ġaltiyāñ kartā hūñ.
lines.id: Thank you. But I still make a lot of mistakes.
lines.literal: thanks. but I now many mistakes do-(m) am.

notes: **Look at اٹھتا ہوں and اٹھتی ہوں — the same sentence, different speakers.** Urdu has no neutral way of saying "I get up": you have to choose. If you're a man, it's always **ـتا**; if you're a woman, always **ـتی**. This isn't politeness or style — it's compulsory grammar, and getting it wrong sounds like you've misdescribed yourself.

**What counts is the gender of the DOER, not of the listener.** A woman talking to a man still says میں جاتی ہوں. A man talking to a woman still says میں جاتا ہوں. This is the one that gets mixed up most in the first month.

**The negative drops ہوں.** Compare میں کھاتا ہوں ("I eat") with میں نہیں کھاتا ("I don't eat"). The word نہیں goes before the verb, and ہوں/ہے/ہیں is usually **dropped**. Putting it back — میں نہیں کھاتا ہوں — isn't wrong, but it sounds emphatic, as if you're denying an accusation.

**Most activities are built with کرنا.** Urdu rarely makes new verbs; it attaches کرنا ("to do") to a noun, much like English "do the dishes" or "make a call". ناشتہ کرنا (to have breakfast, literally "to do breakfast"), کام کرنا (to work), محنت کرنا (to work hard), انتظار کرنا (to wait), مدد کرنا (to help), بات کرنا (to talk). Once you see the pattern, hundreds of verbs open up at once.

**The verb پڑھنا does two things: read and study.** The sentence میں اردو پڑھتا ہوں can mean "I read Urdu" or "I study Urdu", depending on context. The phrase نماز پڑھنا ("to pray") uses it too, because the prayers are recited. The word for "to teach" is پڑھانا — one letter longer.

**The word روز and the parts of the day need no preposition.** The word روز means "every day". Parts of the day take کو — صبح کو (in the morning) · دوپہر کو (at midday) · شام کو (in the evening) · رات کو (at night) — although in fast speech the کو is often dropped.

grammars.title: The habitual: stem + تا/تی/تے + ہوں/ہے/ہیں
body: This is the verb form you'll use most, and it's always built the same way, without exception. Take the dictionary form — say جانا (to go) — drop ـنا, and what's left is the **stem**: جا. Then add the right ending and finish with a form of "to be".
Two things are decided at once: the ending **تا/تی/تے** follows **the gender and number of the doer**, while **ہوں/ہے/ہو/ہیں** follows **the person** (I, he/she, you).
after: ⚠️ Look at the آپ row: even when you're talking to just one person, the form is **plural** — جاتے ہیں for a man. A woman you address respectfully gets جاتی ہیں: the ending ـتی doesn't change in the feminine plural, but the ہیں is plural.
Negative: **نہیں** goes right before the verb, and ہوں/ہے/ہیں is dropped. میں نہیں جاتا · وہ نہیں جاتی · ہم نہیں جاتے.

grammars.title: What the habitual is used for
body: This form covers ground that English splits between the simple present and a few other phrasings, and knowing its limits saves a lot of confusion.

head: Used for
Urdu example
Meaning
rows: پاکستان میں لوگ اردو بولتے ہیں۔
کلاس نو بجے شروع ہوتی ہے۔

after: ⚠️ This form is **not** for something happening right now. "I'm eating" isn't میں کھاتا ہوں but میں کھا رہا ہوں — that's unit 11. Just as in English, if you use the habitual for what's happening at this moment, you'll be understood but it'll sound like you're describing a habit, not the present situation.

blocks.title: A whole day in eight sentences
items: Morning: میں چھ بجے اٹھتا ہوں۔ پھر نہاتا ہوں اور ناشتہ کرتا ہوں۔ ("I get up at six. Then I shower and have breakfast.")
Midday: میں دفتر جاتا ہوں اور کام کرتا ہوں۔ دوپہر کو کھانا کھاتا ہوں۔ ("I go to the office and work. At midday I eat lunch.")
Evening and night: شام کو میں اردو پڑھتا ہوں۔ رات کو کھانا کھاتا ہوں اور گیارہ بجے سوتا ہوں۔ ("In the evening I study Urdu. At night I have dinner and go to bed at eleven.")

If you're a woman, change every ـتا to ـتی, so the sentences become میں چھ بجے اٹھتی ہوں، نہاتی ہوں، ناشتہ کرتی ہوں. Rewrite these eight sentences for yourself — with the times, places, and activities you actually do. It's the most valuable exercise in this unit.
